claims.text: Adding a small, controlled amount of boron to a crystalline or partially ordered metallic alloy enhances its glass-forming ability during rapid solidification.
Boron addition increases atomic-size mismatch in the host alloy.
Boron introduces a strong negative mixing enthalpy into the host alloy.
The atomic-size mismatch and negative mixing enthalpy introduced by boron disrupt crystalline-phase nucleation.
The small size and metalloid character of boron create local compositional inhomogeneities in the alloy.
Boron addition creates local strain fields in the alloy.
Boron-induced compositional inhomogeneities and strain fields destabilize the nucleation and growth of ordered crystalline phases.
Suppression of crystalline nucleation and growth promotes retention of an amorphous structure.
Under identical rapid-cooling conditions, a boron-modified alloy will have less crystallinity and a larger amorphous region than the alloy without boron.
DSC and XRD can be used to assess the predicted change in crystallinity or amorphous content.
The beneficial effect of boron requires chemical compatibility with the host alloy and an optimized boron concentration.
Excessive or chemically incompatible boron additions may produce undesirable phases.
The optimal boron concentration and magnitude of glass-forming-ability enhancement vary among alloy systems.
